title: RBI Bans Lenders From Selling Seized Assets Back to Defaulting Borrowers
excerpt: New prudential norms under the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025 prohibit banks, small finance banks, and NBFCs from selling acquired non-financial assets back to defaulters or their related parties, effective October 2026.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • RBI prohibits lenders from selling seized assets back to defaulting borrowers or related parties.
  • Lenders must auction seized assets within seven years, following board-approved policies.
  • New norms take effect on October 1, 2026, with legacy assets due by September 30, 2027.
  • Specified non-financial assets will be disclosed separately in balance sheets, not affecting NPA ratios.

  • Banks, small finance banks, and NBFCs are barred from selling specified non-financial assets (SNFAs) back to defaulting borrowers or their related parties, even after the asset is no longer classified as an SNFA.
  • Lenders must dispose of seized immovable assets within a maximum of seven years through public auctions, with board-approved policies governing the entire process.
  • The norms take effect October 1, 2026, with legacy assets required to comply by September 30, 2027.
  • SNFAs will be disclosed separately in balance sheets and excluded from gross NPA, net NPA, and provisioning coverage ratios.

What the RBI Ordered

The Reserve Bank of India has issued final prudential norms under the Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, closing a longstanding loophole in India's stressed asset resolution framework. The directive, released on July 16, prohibits banks, small finance banks, and non-banking financial companies from selling specified non-financial assets — primarily immovable property seized during loan recovery — back to the borrowers who defaulted on those loans in the first place.

The restriction extends to related parties of the defaulting borrower, as defined under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. Critically, the ban remains in place even after an asset ceases to be classified as an SNFA or is reclassified for the lender's own use.

"A SNFA shall not be sold back to the borrower or its related parties. Related parties shall have the same meaning as defined in the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016."

- Reserve Bank of India, Stressed Assets Directions

How the Framework Works

Under the new norms, a specified non-financial asset is defined as an immovable asset that a lender acquires — through legal or contractual mechanisms — to fully or partially satisfy its claims against a borrower whose account has been classified as a non-performing asset (NPA). For commercial banks, this includes non-banking assets acquired under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

Lenders can acquire such assets only as a last resort, after all other recovery options have been explored and deemed unviable. When a lender acquires an SNFA against partial extinguishment of a loan, the remaining exposure is treated as a restructured loan under existing prudential norms.

The RBI has set a maximum holding period of seven years for these assets. Disposal must follow public auction processes aligned with the principles of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. At least two independent external valuers must determine the distress sale value, and lenders must record SNFAs at the lower of the net book value of the extinguished exposure or this assessed distress value.

Board-Level Governance Required

Every regulated entity must adopt a board-approved policy covering SNFA acquisition and disposal. These policies must specify limits on such assets as a share of total assets, eligibility criteria, delegation of authority, recovery efforts to be attempted before acquisition, and a disposal timeline not exceeding seven years.

The governance requirement aims to prevent ad hoc decisions by branch or mid-level management. Each acquisition must meet the board-level framework before proceeding.

The Moral Hazard Problem

The sell-back prohibition mirrors a principle embedded in Section 29A of the IBC, which bars defaulting promoters and connected persons from bidding for their own companies during insolvency proceedings.

"Conceptually, this mirrors IBC's Section 29A policy concern that defaulting promoters or connected persons should not regain assets through the back door."

- Rohit Jain, Managing Partner, Singhania & Co.

Without this restriction, a borrower could default on a loan, allow the bank to seize the collateral property, and then repurchase it — potentially at a discount — through a direct sale or via related parties. The RBI's absolute ban eliminates this possibility, though some legal experts have noted it could depress price discovery in cases where the borrower is the highest-value user of the property.

Legacy Assets and Disclosure

For assets already on lenders' books, the RBI has built in a transition period. SNFAs outstanding as of September 30, 2026 — classified as "legacy SNFAs" — must comply with the new framework by September 30, 2027.

In a significant accounting change, SNFAs will not be counted as part of gross NPAs, net NPAs, stressed exposures, or provisioning coverage ratios. Instead, banks and NBFCs must disclose them under separate accounting heads in their balance sheets, giving investors and regulators clearer visibility into the nature of these holdings.

What This Means for NRIs and the Diaspora

For non-resident Indians with property investments in India — whether directly held or through family — the new norms add a layer of protection. Properties seized as part of NPA resolution cannot be quietly sold back to defaulting parties through related-party transactions, making the disposal process more transparent. NRI investors in Indian banking stocks should also note the accounting shift: the separate disclosure of SNFAs will provide a cleaner picture of actual asset quality when evaluating bank balance sheets.

What Comes Next

The norms take effect on October 1, 2026, giving lenders roughly two and a half months to finalize board-approved policies and align internal processes. The one-year grace period for legacy assets means the full impact on bank balance sheets will become visible in annual results for the fiscal year ending March 2028. Legal experts expect the framework to accelerate disposal of seized properties sitting on lender books, while the absolute ban on sell-backs may face challenge from borrowers arguing it limits their ability to reclaim their assets at fair value.

Impact on Lenders and Borrowers
›Prohibition prevents borrowers from reclaiming assets through related parties.
›Lenders must adopt board-approved policies for asset acquisition and disposal.
›New norms enhance transparency for NRI property investments.
›Framework aims to accelerate disposal of seized properties.
